isch-flat.title: Ischemic Stroke: What Happens in the First 24 Hours
isch-flat.subtitle: CBF, OEF & the Penumbra
isch-flat.description: By 24 hours, blood flow at the center of an ischemic stroke drops below 20% of normal. Here's how it gets there, step by step.
points: How the brain compensates first: arteriolar dilation, rising OEF, CBV and MTT (Fig. 3.7)
Core vs rim: why flow falls most in the central territory and collaterals protect the edges
The timeline: CBF, CMRO₂ and OEF from 1 hour to 24 hours and beyond
The rim of high oxygen extraction, lasting up to 16 hours, and its variable fate
Spontaneous recanalization, luxury perfusion, and the chronic infarct
isch-flat.audience: For medical and pharmacy education: neurology, neuropharmacology and USMLE / NAPLEX / PLAB revision.
credits: Source: Stroke: Pathophysiology, Diagnosis, and Management, 7th ed. (Grotta et al., Elsevier), pp. 30–31, paraphrased. Graphs are schematic, after Fig. 3.7.
Music includes the Salamander Grand Piano by Alexander Holm (CC BY 3.0).
Educational content only, not medical advice.

cbf.title: Cerebral Autoregulation Explained: How the Brain Holds Its Blood Flow
cbf.subtitle: CPP, CVR & Carotid Stenosis
cbf.description: Between 70 and 150 mmHg of perfusion pressure, cerebral blood flow barely changes. Here's how the brain does it, and when it fails.
points: The autoregulation plateau: flow falls ≤ 18%, then steeply outside 70–150 mmHg
The lever: arteriolar diameter, cerebrovascular resistance (CVR), a ~10 s lag, and the rise in CBV
Myogenic vs metabolic control: why local oxygen wins in vivo
Chronic hypertension shifts the curve: lower limit 100–120 mmHg, and why that matters for ischemia
Local CPP, not MAP: CPP = MAP − ICP
Finite capacity: autoregulation lost in hypercapnia, anemia, hypoxemia
Carotid stenosis: no effect until 60–70%, and the role of collaterals
cbf.audience: For medical and pharmacy students: neurology, physiology, and USMLE / NAPLEX / PLAB revision.
credits: Source: Stroke: Pathophysiology, Diagnosis, and Management, 7th ed. (Grotta et al., Elsevier), pp. 29–30, paraphrased. Curves are schematic.
Educational content only, not medical advice.

thrombus-news.title: Thrombus Formation in 60 Seconds
thrombus-news.subtitle: Real Histology
thrombus-news.description: About three quarters of this clot is pale fibrin, and only a quarter red cells. Real microscope images show how a thrombus is built, and why that matters for clot-dissolving drugs.
points: A real clot cut open: layered bands of fibrin and red cells
Up close: the fibrin net that traps red cells (electron micrograph)
Fast arterial flow → platelet-rich clots; slow flow → fibrin-rich
The chain: tenase and prothrombinase on the platelet surface → thrombin → fibrin, cross-linked by factor XIIIa
t-PA and plasmin break fibrin down, and why fibrin content and cross-linking may affect how well clot-dissolving drugs work
thrombus-news.audience: For medical and pharmacy students: hematology, stroke, and USMLE / NAPLEX / PLAB revision.
credits: Source: Stroke: Pathophysiology, Diagnosis, and Management, 7th ed. (Grotta et al., Elsevier), Ch. 2, "Thrombus formation", paraphrased.
Images: Mikael Häggström, M.D. (CC0); Janice Carr, CDC (public domain).
The 74% / 26% split is a colour count on one slide, an estimate (about ±3%), not a lab measurement.
Educational content only, not medical advice.
